extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students (and instructors) studying discrete mathematics; readers of the textbook's solutions manual
extracted.subtask_description: Worked solutions and proof-patterns for standard discrete-math exercises (sets, relations, functions, induction, combinatorics, sequences). The page gives methods, hints, and example constructions used to prove or disprove textbook-level statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove a function is one-to-one
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that if f(x1) = f(x2) then x1 = x2 (assume equality of outputs and deduce equality of inputs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical pattern: Suppose x1,x2 ∈ domain and f(x1)=f(x2); perform algebraic manipulation to conclude x1=x2. Example given: manipulate (x+1)/(x−1) equality to deduce x1=x2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove a function is onto (surjective)
rubrics_metrics.description: For an arbitrary y in the codomain construct or solve for x in the domain such that f(x) = y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical pattern: let y be arbitrary in codomain, solve equation f(x)=y to obtain x (give explicit formula) and check x belongs to domain. Example: invert rational formula by algebra to produce preimage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show a relation or function composition is well-defined / is a function
rubrics_metrics.description: To show S ◦ R is a function, demonstrate uniqueness of second coordinate given first: if (a,c) and (a,c') are in S◦R then c = c'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pattern: pick representative preimage a for b using Ran(R)=B, trace through composition and use functional uniqueness to conclude equality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use counterexamples to disprove general statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide explicit finite sets/functions/relations that violate the claimed property to show the statement is false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided: small sets A,B,C and explicitly listed pairs for R,f to show statements like 'f is not a function' or 'property fails'. Construct minimal examples to demonstrate failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show relation properties: reflexive, transitive, antisymmetric
rubrics_metrics.description: Check the defining condition for each property on arbitrary elements or pairs: (x,x) ∈ R for reflexive; (x,y),(y,z)∈R ⇒ (x,z)∈R for transitive; (x,y),(y,x)∈R ⇒ x=y for antisymmetric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply definition directly, often restricting attention to subsets (e.g., R ∩ (A'×A')) and using closure or minimality hypotheses. Break into cases when needed (e.g., special distinguished element a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove transitivity and reflexivity of induced/restricted relations
rubrics_metrics.description: When restricting a relation R to A'×A' (R_A'), prove reflexivity/transitivity/antisymmetry by verifying original properties hold on A'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show each defining condition for R_A' by using membership in R and that elements lie in A'. Use case analysis when adding extra pairs (e.g., union with {a}×A).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove closure under a function (smallest closed set containing B)
rubrics_metrics.description: To show C is closed under f and is the smallest such superset of B, prove B⊆C⊆A, show ∀x∈C(f(x)∈C), and prove any other closed D with B⊆D must contain C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two constructions shown: (a) intersection of all closed supersets (∩F) and (b) union of iterates ∪ B_n with inductive proof B_n ⊆ D for any closed D.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by (ordinary) induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish base case(s) then assume statement for n (or up to n for strong induction) and prove for n+1; manipulate algebraic expressions accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical steps shown: verify base case, assume formula for n, add the (n+1)st term or multiply as needed, simplify to reach closed form. Examples: sum formulas, combinatorial identities, factorial/inequality proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by strong induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume the statement holds for all m < n and use those assumptions to prove the statement for n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used when the n+1 proof depends on multiple earlier cases (e.g., establishing minimal counterexample contradictions or enumerative constructions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Show big-O membership and properties of O relation
rubrics_metrics.description: To show f ∈ O(g) choose a ∈ Z+ and c>0 such that ∀x>a, |f(x)| ≤ c|g(x)|. To show reflexivity/transitivity of the O-relation use trivial bounds and composition of constants; to show non-membership, derive contradiction by choosing large x.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: prove f(x)=7x+3 ∈ O(x^2) with explicit constants; show g∉O(f) by assuming constants exist and choosing x large enough to contradict the inequality. Prove that O defines a reflexive, transitive relation but not antisymmetric by explicit examples (f(x)=x, g(x)=2x).

rubrics_metrics.name: Show linear combinations preserve O-relations
rubrics_metrics.description: If f1 ∈ O(g) and f2 ∈ O(g), then for s,t ∈ R the linear combination s f1 + t f2 ∈ O(g).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose bounds for f1 and f2, pick a = max(a1,a2), set c = |s|c1 + |t|c2 + 1 (ensure positivity) and bound |s f1 + t f2| ≤ c|g| for x>a.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting subsets and binomial identities by induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove P(A) has 2^n elements by induction splitting subsets into those containing a given element and those that do not. Prove Pascal identity and binomial theorem via combinatorial/inductive steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use induction with cases k=0, k=n+1, and 0<k≤n; show combinatorial splitting into subsets with/without a distinguished element; use Pascal identity to induct the binomial theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use algebraic manipulation to show function/composition identities
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute f(g(x)) and g(f(x)) algebraically to show compositions equal identity or other target expressions, thereby proving inverses or bijectivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: explicitly compute rational/log expressions to verify f◦g = id and g◦f = id and conclude f is bijection and inverse is g.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct explicit bijections to prove sets denumerable or equal cardinality
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide explicit formulas for functions (e.g., f(n)=n−1 or pairing functions f(i,j)) and prove they are one-to-one and onto to establish bijections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical verification: prove injectivity via algebraic identities and surjectivity by constructing preimages (possibly using minimality/k selection). Examples include bijections between Z+ and N, Cantor-style pairing function proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show R^n corresponds to R-paths of length n
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove by induction that (a,b)∈R^n iff there exists an R-path f from a to b of length n (i.e., sequence f(0)=a,...,f(n)=b with consecutive pairs in R).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Base case n=1 trivial; induction step uses decomposition into R1◦R^n and appending/removing final pair to/from path.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove properties of finite sets and cardinality via bijections with In
rubrics_metrics.description: A set A is finite iff there exists n with In ∼ A; uniqueness of n follows by comparing bijections; subsets of finite sets are finite with size ≤ |A|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use induction on n for subset results. Show construction of bijections and apply previous uniqueness lemma.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use minimal counterexample / descent arguments for irrationality
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume rationality p/q in lowest terms, derive parity/congruence contradictions leading to a smaller representative, contradicting minimality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shown in proof that √6 is irrational: derive that both p and q are even, contradicting minimality of denominator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove inequalities (e.g., AM-GM) via pairing and induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Use algebraic manipulation (set m=(a+b)/2, d=(a−b)/2) to show √(ab) ≤ (a+b)/2 for two numbers, then extend to longer lists by induction (pairing into two groups).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Base case for length 2, then use induction on list length with splitting into two equal parts and applying inductive hypothesis and AM-GM for products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show partial orders extend to total orders via iterative extension
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a countable enumerated set, build an increasing sequence of partial orders Rn that eventually compare each listed element with all previously considered ones; union yields a total order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct Rn so R = R0 ⊆ R1 ⊆ ... and enforce ∀i∈In ∀j((ai,aj)∈Rn ∨ (aj,ai)∈Rn); union preserves reflexivity, transitivity, antisymmetry and yields comparability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove divisibility identities by induction
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove statements like (i+2) | (x+i) for specified ranges, use base case and assume divisibility for n then show for n+1 by algebraic manipulation and factorization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: show for all 0≤i≤n, (i+2)|((n+2)!+2+i) by expressing (n+2)!+2+i in terms of (n+1)!+2+i and factoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derive closed-form formulas for linear recurrences using characteristic equation
rubrics_metrics.description: Solve quadratic/characteristic equation for constants c (roots), express general term as combination s c1^n + t c2^n, determine s,t from initial conditions and verify by induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Gibonacci sequences with characteristic c^2 = 1 + c give c = (1±√5)/2 and determine coefficients s,t using initial terms; verify recurrence holds for all n.
